name: Atomic structure and the Periodic Table

statementText.1.1: know the structure of an atom in terms of electrons, protons and neutrons
statementText.1.2: know the relative mass and relative charge of protons, neutrons and electrons
statementText.1.3: know what is meant by the terms ‘atomic (proton) number’ and ‘mass number’
statementText.1.4: be able to determine the number of each type of sub-atomic particle in an atom, molecule or ion from the atomic (proton) number and mass number
statementText.1.6: be able to define the terms ‘relative isotopic mass’ and ‘relative atomic mass’, based on the ^12C scale
statementText.1.7: understand the terms ‘relative molecular mass’ and ‘relative formula mass’, including calculating these values from relative atomic masses [Definitions of these terms will not be expected. The term ‘relative formula mass’ should be used for compounds with giant structures.]
statementText.1.8: be able to analyse and interpret data from mass spectrometry to calculate relative atomic mass from relative abundance of isotopes and vice versa
statementText.1.9: be able to predict the mass spectra, including relative peak heights, for diatomic molecules, including chlorine
statementText.1.10: understand how mass spectrometry can be used to determine the relative molecular mass of a molecule [Limited to the m/z value for the molecular ion, M^+, giving the relative molecular mass of the molecule.]
statementText.1.11: be able to define the terms ‘first ionisation energy’ and ‘successive ionisation energies’
statementText.1.12: understand how ionisation energies are influenced by the number of protons, the electron shielding and the electron sub-shell from which the electron is removed
statementText.1.13: understand reasons for the general increase in first ionisation energy across a period
statementText.1.14: understand reasons for the decrease in first ionisation energy down a group
statementText.1.15: understand how ideas about electronic configuration developed from: • i the fact that atomic emission spectra provide evidence for the existence of quantum shells • ii the fact that successive ionisation energies provide evidence for the existence of quantum shells and the group to which the element belongs • iii the fact that the first ionisation energy of successive elements provides evidence for electron sub-shells
statementText.1.16: know the number of electrons that can fill the first four quantum shells
statementText.1.17: know that an orbital is a region within an atom that can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins
statementText.1.18: know the shape of an s-orbital and a p-orbital
statementText.1.19: know the number of electrons that occupy s, p and d-subshells
statementText.1.20: know that electrons fill subshells singly, before pairing up, and that two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins
statementText.1.21: be able to predict the electronic configurations, using 1s notation and electrons- in-boxes notation, of: • i atoms, given the atomic number, Z, up to Z = 36 • ii ions, given the atomic number, Z, and the ionic charge, for s and p block ions only, up to Z = 36
statementText.1.22: know that elements can be classified as s, p and d-block elements
statementText.1.23: understand that electronic configuration determines the chemical properties of an element
statementText.1.24: understand periodicity in terms of a repeating pattern across different periods
statementText.1.25: understand reasons for the trends in the following properties of the elements from periods 2 and 3 of the Periodic Table: • i the melting and boiling temperatures of the elements, based on given data, in terms of structure and bonding • ii ionisation energy based on given data or recall of the plots of ionisation energy versus atomic number
statementText.1.26: be able to illustrate periodicity using data, including electronic configurations, atomic radii, melting and boiling temperatures and first ionisation energies

statementText.2.1: know that ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
statementText.2.2: understand the effects that ionic radius and ionic charge have on the strength of ionic bonding
statementText.2.3: understand the formation of ions in terms of electron loss or gain
statementText.2.4: be able to draw electronic configuration diagrams of cations and anions using dot-and-cross diagrams
statementText.2.5: understand reasons for the trends in ionic radii down a group and for a set of isoelectronic ions, e.g. N^3– to Al^3+
statementText.2.6: understand that the physical properties of ionic compounds and the migration of ions provide evidence for the existence of ions
statementText.2.7: know that a covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between two nuclei and the shared pair of electrons between them
statementText.2.8: be able to draw dot-and-cross diagrams to show electrons in covalent substances, including: • i molecules with single, double and triple bonds • ii species exhibiting dative covalent (coordinate) bonding, including Al2Cl6 and ammonium ion
statementText.2.9: understand the relationship between bond lengths and bond strengths for covalent bonds
statementText.2.10: understand that the shape of a simple molecule or ion is determined by the repulsion between the electron pairs that surround a central atom
statementText.2.11: understand reasons for the shapes of, and bond angles in, simple molecules and ions with up to six outer pairs of electrons (any combination of bonding pairs and lone pairs) [Examples should include BeCl2, BCl3, CH4, NH3, NH4^+, H2O, CO2, PCl5(g) and SF6(g) and related molecules and ions; as well as simple organic molecules in this specification.]
statementText.2.12: be able to predict the shapes of, and bond angles in, simple molecules and ions analogous to those specified above using electron-pair repulsion theory
statementText.2.13: know that electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract the bonding electrons in a covalent bond
statementText.2.14: know that ionic and covalent bonding are the extremes of a continuum of bonding type and that electronegativity differences lead to bond polarity in bonds and molecules
statementText.2.15: understand that molecules with polar bonds may not be polar molecules and be able to predict whether or not a given molecule is likely to be polar
statementText.2.16: understand the nature of intermolecular forces resulting from the following interactions: • i London forces (instantaneous dipole – induced dipole) • ii permanent dipoles • iii hydrogen bonds
statementText.2.17: understand the interactions in molecules, such as H2O, liquid NH3 and liquid HF, which give rise to hydrogen bonding
statementText.2.18: understand the following anomalous properties of water resulting from hydrogen bonding: • i its relatively high melting temperature and boiling temperature • ii the density of ice compared to that of water
statementText.2.19: be able to predict the presence of hydrogen bonding in molecules analogous to those mentioned above
statementText.2.20: understand, in terms of intermolecular forces, physical properties shown by materials, including: • i the trends in boiling temperatures of alkanes with increasing chain length • ii the effect of branching in the carbon chain on the boiling temperatures of alkanes • iii the relatively low volatility (higher boiling temperatures) of alcohols compared to alkanes with a similar number of electrons • iv the trends in boiling temperatures of the hydrogen halides, HF to HI
statementText.2.21: understand factors that influence the choice of solvents, including: • i water, to dissolve some ionic compounds, in terms of the hydration of the ions • ii water, to dissolve simple alcohols, in terms of hydrogen bonding • iii water, as a poor solvent for compounds (to include polar molecules such as halogenoalkanes), in terms of inability to form hydrogen bonds • iv non-aqueous solvents, for compounds that have similar intermolecular forces to those in the solvent
statementText.2.22: know that metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between metal ions and the delocalised electrons

statementText.2.23: know that giant lattices are present in: • i ionic solids (giant ionic lattices) • ii covalently bonded solids, such as diamond, graphite and silicon(IV) oxide (giant covalent lattices) • iii solid metals (giant metallic lattices)
statementText.2.24: know that the structure of covalently bonded substances such as iodine, I2, and ice, H2O, is simple molecular
statementText.2.25: know the different structures formed by carbon atoms, including graphite, diamond and graphene
statementText.2.26: be able to predict the type of structure and bonding present in a substance from numerical data and/or other information
statementText.2.27: be able to predict the physical properties of a substance, including melting and boiling temperature, electrical conductivity and solubility in water, in terms of: • i the types of particle present (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons) • ii the structure of the substance • iii the type of bonding and the presence of intermolecular forces, where relevant

statementText.3.1: know what is meant by the term ‘oxidation number’
statementText.3.2: be able to calculate the oxidation number of elements in compounds and ions [The use of oxidation numbers in peroxides and metal hydrides is expected.]
statementText.3.3: understand oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer and changes in oxidation number, applied to reactions of s- and p-block elements
statementText.3.4: understand oxidation and reduction in terms of electron loss or electron gain
statementText.3.5: know that oxidising agents gain electrons
statementText.3.6: know that reducing agents lose electrons
statementText.3.7: understand that a disproportionation reaction involves an element in a single species being simultaneously oxidised and reduced
statementText.3.8: know that oxidation number is a useful concept in terms of the classification of reactions as redox and as disproportionation
statementText.3.9: be able to indicate the oxidation number of an element in a compound or ion, using a Roman numeral
statementText.3.10: be able to write formulae given oxidation numbers
statementText.3.11: understand that metals, in general, form positive ions by loss of electrons with an increase in oxidation number
statementText.3.12: understand that non-metals, in general, form negative ions by gain of electrons with a decrease in oxidation number
statementText.3.13: be able to write ionic half-equations and use them to construct full ionic equations

statementText.4.1: understand reasons for the trend in ionisation energy down Group 2
statementText.4.2: understand reasons for the trend in reactivity of the Group 2 elements down the group
statementText.4.3: know the reactions of the elements Mg to Ba in Group 2 with oxygen, chlorine and water
statementText.4.4: know the reactions of the oxides of Group 2 elements with water and dilute acid, and their hydroxides with dilute acid
statementText.4.5: know the trends in solubility of the hydroxides and sulfates of Group 2 elements
statementText.4.6: understand reasons for the trends in thermal stability of the nitrates and the carbonates of the elements in Groups 1 and 2 in terms of the size and charge of the cations involved
statementText.4.7: understand the formation of characteristic flame colours by Group 1 and 2 compounds in terms of electron transitions [Students will be expected to know the flame colours for Groups 1 and 2 compounds.]
statementText.4.8: understand experimental procedures to show: • i patterns in thermal decomposition of Group 1 and 2 nitrates and carbonates • ii flame colours in compounds of Group 1 and 2 elements

statementText.4.9: understand reasons for the trends in melting and boiling temperatures, physical state at room temperature, and electronegativity for Group 7 elements
statementText.4.10: understand reasons for the trend in reactivity of Group 7 elements down the group
statementText.4.11: understand the trend in reactivity of Group 7 elements in terms of the redox reactions of Cl2, Br2 and I2 with halide ions in aqueous solution, followed by the addition of an organic solvent
statementText.4.12: understand, in terms of changes in oxidation number, the following reactions of the halogens: • i oxidation reactions with Group 1 and 2 metals • ii the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with water and the use of chlorine in water treatment • iii the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide to form bleach • iv the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with hot alkali • v reactions analogous to those specified above
statementText.4.13: understand the following reactions: • i solid Group 1 halides with concentrated sulfuric acid, to illustrate the trend in reducing ability of the hydrogen halides • ii precipitation reactions of the aqueous anions Cl^–, Br^– and I^– with aqueous silver nitrate solution, followed by aqueous ammonia solution • iii hydrogen halides with ammonia and with water (to produce acids)
statementText.4.14: be able to make predictions about fluorine and astatine and their compounds, in terms of knowledge of trends in halogen chemistry

statementText.4.15: know reactions, including ionic equations where appropriate, for identifying: • i carbonate ions, CO3^2-, and hydrogencarbonate ions, HCO3^–, using an aqueous acid to form carbon dioxide • ii sulfate ions, SO4^2-, using acidified barium chloride solution • iii ammonium ions, NH4^+, using sodium hydroxide solution and warming to form ammonia [Tests for halide ions and for the ions of Group 1 and 2 metals are also required, but are covered elsewhere in this Topic.]

name: Formulae, equations and amounts of substance

statementText.5.1: know that the mole (mol) is the unit for amount of a substance
statementText.5.2: be able to use the Avogadro constant, L, (6.02 × 10^23 mol^-1) in calculations
statementText.5.3: know that the molar mass of a substance is the mass per mole of the substance in g mol^-1
statementText.5.4: know what is meant by the terms ‘empirical formula’ and ‘molecular formula’
statementText.5.5: be able to use experimental data to calculate • i. empirical formulae • ii. molecular formulae including the use of pV = nRT for gases and volatile liquids [Calculations of empirical formula may involve composition by mass or percentage composition by mass data.]
statementText.5.6: be able to write balanced full and ionic equations, including state symbols, for chemical reactions
statementText.5.7: be able to calculate amounts of substances (in mol) in reactions involving mass, volume of gas, volume of solution and concentration [These calculations may involve reactants and/or products.]
statementText.5.8: be able to calculate reacting masses from chemical equations, and vice versa, using the concepts of amount of substance and molar mass
statementText.5.9: be able to calculate reacting volumes of gases from chemical equations, and vice versa, using the concepts of amount of substance
statementText.5.10: be able to calculate reacting volumes of gases from chemical equations, and vice versa, using the concepts of molar volume of gases
statementText.5.11: be able to calculate solution concentrations, in mol dm^-3 and g dm^-3, including simple acid-base titrations using a range of acids, alkalis and indicators [The use of both phenolphthalein and methyl orange as indicators will be expected.]
statementText.5.12: be able to: • i calculate measurement uncertainties and measurement errors in experimental results • ii comment on sources of error in experimental procedures
statementText.5.13: understand how to minimise the percentage error and percentage uncertainty in experiments involving measurements
statementText.5.14: be able to calculate percentage yields and percentage atom economies using chemical equations and experimental results molar mass of the desired product Atom economy of a reaction = × 100% sum of the molar masses of all products
statementText.5.15: be able to relate ionic and full equations, with state symbols, to observations from simple test tube reactions, to include: • i displacement reactions • ii reactions of acids • iii precipitation reactions
statementText.5.16: understand risks and hazards in practical procedures and suggest appropriate precautions where necessary

statementText.6.1: know that a hydrocarbon is a compound of hydrogen and carbon only
statementText.6.2: be able to represent organic molecules using empirical formulae, molecular formulae, general formulae, structural formulae, displayed formulae and skeletal formulae
statementText.6.3: know what is meant by the terms ‘homologous series’ and ‘functional group’
statementText.6.4: be able to name compounds relevant to this specification using the rules of International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) nomenclature [Students will be expected to know prefixes for compounds up to C10]
statementText.6.5: be able to classify reactions as addition, elimination, substitution, oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis or polymerisation
statementText.6.6: understand the term ‘structural isomerism’ and determine the possible structural, displayed and skeletal formulae of an organic molecule, given its molecular formula
statementText.6.7: understand the term ‘stereoisomerism’, as illustrated by E/Z isomerism (including cis-trans isomerism where two of the substituent groups are the same)

statementText.6.8: know the general formula for alkanes
statementText.6.9: know that alkanes and cycloalkanes are saturated hydrocarbons
statementText.6.10: understand that alkane fuels are obtained from the fractional distillation, cracking and reforming of crude oil [Reforming is described as the processing of straight-chain hydrocarbons into branched-chain alkanes and cyclic hydrocarbons for efficient combustion.]
statementText.6.11: know that pollutants, including carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and sulfur, carbon particulates and unburned hydrocarbons, are formed during the combustion of alkane fuels
statementText.6.12: understand the problems arising from pollutants from the combustion of fuels, limited to the toxicity of carbon monoxide and the acidity of oxides of nitrogen and sulfur
statementText.6.13: understand how the use of a catalytic converter solves some problems caused by pollutants
statementText.6.14: understand the use of alternative fuels, including biodiesel and alcohols derived from renewable sources such as plants, in terms of a comparison with non-renewable fossil fuels
statementText.6.15: know that a radical: • i is a species with an unpaired electron and is represented in mechanisms by a single dot • ii is formed by homolytic fission of a covalent bond and results in the formation of radicals
statementText.6.16: understand the reactions of alkanes with: • i oxygen in air (combustion) • ii halogens, in terms of the mechanism of radical substitution through initiation, propagation and termination steps [The use of curly half-arrows is not expected in this mechanism.]
statementText.6.17: understand the limitations of the use of radical substitution reactions in the synthesis of organic molecules, in terms of further substitution reactions and the formation of a mixture of products

statementText.6.18: know the general formula for alkenes
statementText.6.19: know that alkenes and cycloalkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons
statementText.6.20: understand the bonding in alkenes in terms of σ- and π- bonds
statementText.6.21: know what is meant by the term ‘electrophile’
statementText.6.22: understand the addition reactions of alkenes with: • i hydrogen, in the presence of a nickel catalyst, to form an alkane • ii halogens to produce dihalogenoalkanes • iii hydrogen halides to produce halogenoalkanes • iv steam, in the presence of an acid catalyst, to produce alcohols • v potassium manganate(VII), in acid conditions, to oxidise the double bond and produce a diol [Knowledge of the application of this reaction to the manufacture of margarine by catalytic hydrogenation of unsaturated vegetable oils is expected.]
statementText.6.23: understand that heterolytic bond fission of a covalent bond results in the formation of ions
statementText.6.24: understand the mechanism of the electrophilic addition reactions between alkenes and: • i halogens • ii hydrogen halides, including addition to unsymmetrical alkenes • iii other given binary compounds [Use of the curly arrow notation is expected − curly arrows should start from either a bond or from a lone pair of electrons. Knowledge of the relative stability of primary, secondary and tertiary carbocation intermediates is expected.]
statementText.6.25: know the qualitative test for a C=C double bond using bromine or bromine water
statementText.6.26: know that alkenes form polymers through addition polymerisation [Be able to identify the repeat unit of an addition polymer given the monomer, and vice versa.]
statementText.6.27: know that waste polymers can be separated into specific types of polymer for: • i recycling • ii incineration to release energy • iii use as a feedstock for cracking
statementText.6.28: understand, in terms of the use of energy and resources over the life cycle of polymer products, that chemists can contribute to the more sustainable use of materials
statementText.6.29: understand how chemists limit the problems caused by polymer disposal by: • i developing biodegradable polymers • ii removing toxic waste gases caused by incineration of plastics

statementText.6.30: know that halogenoalkanes can be classified as primary, secondary or tertiary
statementText.6.31: understand what is meant by the term ‘nucleophile’
statementText.6.32: understand the reactions of halogenoalkanes with: • i aqueous potassium hydroxide to produce alcohols (where the hydroxide ion acts as a nucleophile) • ii aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol (where water acts as a nucleophile) • iii potassium cyanide to produce nitriles (where the cyanide ion acts as a nucleophile) • iv ammonia to produce primary amines (where the ammonia molecule acts as a nucleophile) • v ethanolic potassium hydroxide to produce alkenes (where the hydroxide ion acts as a base) [Students should know this as an example of increasing the length of the carbon chain.]
statementText.6.33: understand that experimental observations and data can be used to compare the relative rates of hydrolysis of: • i primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes • ii chloro-, bromo-, and iodoalkanes using aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol
statementText.6.34: know the trend in reactivity of primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes
statementText.6.35: understand, in terms of bond enthalpy, the trend in reactivity of chloro-, bromo-, and iodoalkanes
statementText.6.36: understand the mechanisms of the nucleophilic substitution reactions between primary halogenoalkanes and: • i aqueous potassium hydroxide • ii ammonia

statementText.6.37: know that alcohols can be classified as primary, secondary or tertiary
statementText.6.38: understand the reactions of alcohols with: • i oxygen in air (combustion) • ii halogenating agents: • PCl5 to produce chloroalkanes • 50% concentrated sulfuric acid and potassium bromide to produce bromoalkanes • red phosphorus and iodine to produce iodoalkanes • iii potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid to oxidise primary alcohols to aldehydes (including a test for the aldehyde using Benedict’s/Fehling’s solution) and carboxylic acids, and secondary alcohols to ketones • iv concentrated phosphoric acid to form alkenes by elimination [In equations, the oxidising agent can be represented as [O]. Descriptions of the mechanisms of these reactions are not expected.]
statementText.6.39: understand the following techniques used in the preparation and purification of a liquid organic compound: • i heating under reflux • ii extraction with a solvent in a separating funnel • iii distillation • iv drying with an anhydrous salt • v boiling temperature determination

name: Modern analytical techniques I: mass spectrometry and infrared

statementText.7.1: be able to use data from a mass spectrometer to: • i determine the relative molecular mass of an organic compound from the molecular ion peak • ii suggest possible structures of a simple organic compound from the m/z of the molecular ion and fragmentation patterns
statementText.7.2: be able to use data from infrared spectra to deduce functional groups present in organic compounds and to predict infrared absorptions, given wavenumber data, due to familiar functional groups, including: • i C–H stretching absorption in alkanes, alkenes and aldehydes • ii C=C stretching absorption in alkenes • iii O–H stretching absorption in alcohols • iv C=O stretching absorption in aldehydes and ketones • v C=O stretching absorption and the broad O-H stretching absorption in carboxylic acids • vi N–H stretching absorption in amines

statementText.8.1: know that standard conditions are 100 kPa and a specified temperature, usually 298 K
statementText.8.2: know that the enthalpy change is the heat energy change measured at constant pressure
statementText.8.3: be able to construct and interpret enthalpy level diagrams showing an enthalpy change, including appropriate signs for exothermic and endothermic reactions [Activation energy is not shown in enthalpy level diagrams but it is shown in reaction profile diagrams.]
statementText.8.4: be able to define standard enthalpy change of: • i reaction • ii formation • iii combustion • iv neutralisation
statementText.8.5: understand experiments to measure enthalpy changes in terms of: • i processing results using the expression: energy transferred = mass x specific heat capacity × temperature change (Q=mcΔT) • ii evaluating sources of error and assumptions made in the experiments o o o [Students will need to consider experiments where: substances are mixed in an insulated container and the temperature change is measured enthalpy of combustion is measured, such as using a series of alcohols in a spirit burner the enthalpy change cannot be measured directly.]
statementText.8.6: be able to calculate enthalpy changes in kJ mol^-1 from given experimental results [Both a sign and units are expected in the final answer.]
statementText.8.7: be able to construct enthalpy cycles using Hess’s Law
statementText.8.8: be able to calculate enthalpy changes from data using Hess’s Law
statementText.8.9: know what is meant by the terms ‘bond enthalpy’ and ‘mean bond enthalpy’
statementText.8.10: be able to calculate an enthalpy change of reaction using mean bond enthalpies and explain the limitations of this method of calculation
statementText.8.11: be able to calculate mean bond enthalpies from enthalpy changes of reaction

statementText.9.1: understand, in terms of collision theory, the effect of a change in concentration, temperature, pressure and surface area on the rate of a chemical reaction
statementText.9.2: understand that reactions only take place when collisions take place with sufficient energy, known as activation energy
statementText.9.3: be able to calculate the rate of a reaction from: • i data showing the time taken for reaction • ii the gradient of a suitable graph, by drawing a tangent, either for initial rate, or at a time, t
statementText.9.4: understand qualitatively, in terms of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies, how changes in temperature affect the rate of a reaction
statementText.9.5: understand the role of catalysts in providing alternative reaction routes of lower activation energy
statementText.9.6: be able to draw the reaction profiles for uncatalysed and catalysed reactions
statementText.9.7: be able to interpret the action of a catalyst in terms of a qualitative understanding of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies
statementText.9.8: understand the use of a solid (heterogeneous) catalyst for industrial reactions, in the gas phase, in terms of providing a surface for the reaction
statementText.9.9: understand the economic benefits of the use of catalysts in industrial reactions

statementText.10.1: know that many reactions are readily reversible and that they can reach a state of dynamic equilibrium in which: • i the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the backward reaction • ii the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant
statementText.10.2: be able to predict and justify the qualitative effect of a change in temperature, concentration or pressure on a homogeneous system in equilibrium
statementText.10.3: evaluate data to explain the necessity, for many industrial processes, to reach a compromise between the yield and the rate of reaction
statementText.10.4: be able to deduce an expression for Kc , for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium concentrations

statementText.11.1: be able to deduce an expression for Kp, for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium partial pressures in atm
statementText.11.2: be able to calculate a value, with units where appropriate, for the equilibrium constant (Kc and Kp) for homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions, from experimental data
statementText.11.3: know the effect of changing temperature on the equilibrium constant (Kc and Kp), for both exothermic and endothermic reactions
statementText.11.4: understand that the effect of temperature on the position of equilibrium is explained using a change in the value of the equilibrium constant
statementText.11.5: understand that the value of the equilibrium constant is not affected by changes in concentration or pressure or by the addition of a catalyst

statementText.12.1: know that a Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor and a Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor
statementText.12.2: know that acid-base reactions involve the transfer of protons
statementText.12.3: be able to identify Brønsted–Lowry conjugate acid-base pairs
statementText.12.4: be able to define the term ‘pH’
statementText.12.5: be able to calculate pH from hydrogen ion concentration
statementText.12.6: be able to calculate the concentration of hydrogen ions, in mol dm^-3, in a solution from its pH, using the expression [H^+] = 10^–pH
statementText.12.7: understand the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid in terms of degree of dissociation
statementText.12.8: be able to calculate the pH of a strong acid
statementText.12.9: be able to deduce the expression for the acid dissociation constant, Ka, for a weak acid and carry out relevant calculations
statementText.12.10: be able to calculate the pH of a weak acid making relevant assumptions
statementText.12.11: be able to define the ionic product of water, Kw
statementText.12.12: be able to calculate the pH of a strong base from its concentration, using Kw
statementText.12.13: be able to define the terms ‘pKa’ and ‘pKw’
statementText.12.14: be able to analyse data from the following experiments: • i measuring the pH of a variety of substances, e.g. equimolar solutions of strong and weak acids, strong and weak bases, and salts • ii comparing the pH of a strong acid and a weak acid after dilution 10, 100 and 1000 times
statementText.12.15: be able to calculate Ka for a weak acid from experimental data given the pH of a solution containing a known mass of acid
statementText.12.16: be able to draw and interpret titration curves using all combinations of strong and weak monobasic acids and bases
statementText.12.17: be able to select a suitable indicator, using a titration curve and appropriate data
statementText.12.18: know what is meant by the term ‘buffer solution’
statementText.12.19: understand the action of a buffer solution
statementText.12.20: be able to calculate the pH of a buffer solution given appropriate data
statementText.12.21: be able to calculate the concentrations of solutions required to prepare a buffer solution of a given pH
statementText.12.22: understand how to use a weak acid–strong base titration curve to: • i demonstrate buffer action • ii determine Ka from the pH at the point where half the acid is neutralised
statementText.12.23: understand why there is a difference in enthalpy changes of neutralisation values for strong and weak acids
statementText.12.24: understand the roles of carbonic acid molecules and hydrogencarbonate ions in controlling the pH of blood

statementText.13.1: be able to define lattice energy as the energy change when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions
statementText.13.2: be able to define the terms: • i enthalpy change of atomisation, ΔatH • ii electron affinity
statementText.13.3: be able to construct Born-Haber cycles and carry out related calculations
statementText.13.4: know that lattice energy provides a measure of ionic bond strength
statementText.13.5: understand that a comparison of the experimental lattice energy value (from a Born-Haber cycle) with the theoretical value (obtained from electrostatic theory) in a particular compound indicates the degree of covalent bonding
statementText.13.6: understand the meaning of polarisation as applied to ions
statementText.13.7: know that the polarising power of a cation depends on its radius and charge
statementText.13.8: know that the polarisability of an anion depends on its radius and charge
statementText.13.9: be able to define the terms ‘enthalpy change of solution, ΔsolH’, and ‘enthalpy change of hydration, ΔhydH’
statementText.13.10: be able to use energy cycles and energy level diagrams to carry out calculations involving enthalpy change of solution, enthalpy change of hydration and lattice energy
statementText.13.11: understand the effect of ionic charge and ionic radius on the values of: • i lattice energy • ii enthalpy change of hydration

statementText.13.12: understand that, since some endothermic reactions can occur at room temperature, enthalpy changes alone do not control whether reactions occur
statementText.13.13: know that entropy is a measure of the disorder of a system and that the natural direction of change is increasing total entropy (positive entropy change)
statementText.13.14: understand why entropy changes occur during: • i changes of state • ii dissolving of a solid ionic lattice • iii reactions in which there is a change in the number of moles from reactants to products o o o o mixing solid barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)2.8H2O, with solid ammonium [Students should be able to discuss typical reactions in terms of disorder and enthalpy change, including: dissolving ammonium nitrate crystals in water reacting ethanoic acid with ammonium carbonate burning magnesium ribbon in air chloride.]
statementText.13.15: understand that the total entropy change in any reaction is the entropy change in the system added to the entropy change in the surroundings, shown by the expression: ΔStotal = ΔSsystem + ΔSsurroundings
statementText.13.16: be able to calculate the entropy change for the system, ΔSsystem , in a reaction, given the entropies of the reactants and products
statementText.13.17: be able to calculate the entropy change in the surroundings, and hence ΔStotal , using the expression: ∆ ∆ = − [H S surroundings T]
statementText.13.18: know that the balance between the entropy change and the enthalpy change determines the feasibility of a reaction and is represented by the equation ΔG = ΔH − TΔSsystem
statementText.13.19: be able to use the equation ΔG = ΔH − TΔSsystem to: • i predict whether a reaction is feasible • ii determine the temperature at which a reaction is feasible
statementText.13.20: be able to use the equation ΔG = −RT ln K to show that reactions which are feasible in terms of ΔG have large values for the equilibrium constant and vice versa
statementText.13.21: understand why a reaction for which the ΔG value is negative may not occur in practice
statementText.13.22: know that reactions that are thermodynamically feasible may be inhibited by kinetic factors

statementText.14.1: understand the terms ‘oxidation’ and ‘reduction’ in terms of electron transfer, applied to s-, p- and d-block elements
statementText.14.2: understand the terms ‘oxidation’ and ‘reduction’ in terms of changes in oxidation number, applied to s-, p- and d-block elements
statementText.14.3: know what is meant by the term ‘standard electrode potential’, E^o
statementText.14.4: know that the standard electrode potential, E^o, refers to conditions of: • i 298 K temperature • ii 100 kPa pressure of gases • iii 1.00 mol dm^-3 concentration of ions
statementText.14.5: know the features of the standard hydrogen electrode and understand why a reference electrode is necessary
statementText.14.6: understand that different methods are used to measure standard electrode potentials of: • i metals or non-metals in contact with their ions in aqueous solution • ii ions of the same element with different oxidation numbers
statementText.14.7: be able to calculate a standard emf, E^o cell, by combining two standard electrode potentials
statementText.14.8: be able to write cell diagrams using the conventional representation of half-cells
statementText.14.9: understand the importance of the conditions when measuring the electrode potential, E
statementText.14.10: be able to predict the thermodynamic feasibility of a reaction using standard electrode potentials
statementText.14.11: understand that E^o cell is directly proportional to the total entropy change and to ln K for a reaction
statementText.14.12: understand the limitations of predictions made using standard electrode potentials, in terms of kinetic inhibition and departure from standard conditions
statementText.14.13: know that standard electrode potentials can be listed as an electrochemical series
statementText.14.14: understand how disproportionation reactions relate to standard electrode potentials
statementText.14.15: understand the application of electrode potentials to storage cells
statementText.14.16: understand that the energy released on the reaction of a fuel with oxygen is utilised in a fuel cell to generate a voltage [Knowledge that methanol and other hydrogen-rich fuels are used in fuel cells is expected.]
statementText.14.17: know the electrode reactions that occur in a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell [Knowledge of hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells with both acidic and alkaline electrolytes is expected.]
statementText.14.18: be able to carry out both structured and non-structured titration calculations including Fe^2+/MnO4^−, and I2/S2O3^2−
statementText.14.19: understand the methods used in redox titrations

statementText.15.1: be able to deduce the electronic configurations of atoms and ions of the d-block elements of period 4 (Sc–Zn), given the atomic number and charge (if any)
statementText.15.2: know that transition metals are d-block elements that form one or more stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals
statementText.15.3: understand why transition metals show variable oxidation number
statementText.15.4: know what is meant by the term ‘ligand’
statementText.15.5: understand that dative (coordinate) bonding is involved in the formation of complex ions
statementText.15.6: know that a complex ion is a central metal ion surrounded by ligands
statementText.15.7: know that transition metals form coloured ions in solution
statementText.15.8: understand that the colour of aqueous ions, and other complex ions, results from the splitting of the energy levels of the d-orbitals by ligands
statementText.15.9: understand why there is a lack of colour in some aqueous ions and other complex ions
statementText.15.10: understand that colour changes in transition metal ions may arise as a result of changes in: • i oxidation number • ii ligand • iii coordination number
statementText.15.11: understand the meaning of the term ‘coordination number’
statementText.15.12: understand why H2O, OH^− and NH3 act as monodentate ligands
statementText.15.13: understand why complexes with six-fold coordination have an octahedral shape, such as those formed by metal ions with H2O, OH^− and NH3 as ligands
statementText.15.14: know that transition metal ions may form tetrahedral complexes with relatively large ligands such as Cl^−
statementText.15.15: know that square planar complexes are also formed by transition metal ions and that cis-platin is an example of such a complex
statementText.15.16: understand why cis-platin used in cancer treatment is supplied as a single isomer and not in a mixture with the trans form
statementText.15.17: be able to identify bidentate ligands, such as NH2CH2CH2NH2 and multidentate ligands, such as EDTA^4−
statementText.15.18: know that haemoglobin is an iron(II) complex containing a multidentate ligand [The structure of the haem group will not be assessed.]
statementText.15.19: know that a ligand exchange reaction occurs when an oxygen molecule bound to haemoglobin is replaced by a carbon monoxide molecule

statementText.15.20: know the colours of the oxidation states of vanadium (+5, +4, +3 and +2) in its compounds
statementText.15.21: understand redox reactions for the interconversion of the oxidation states of vanadium (+5, +4, +3 and +2), in terms of the relevant E^o values
statementText.15.22: understand, in terms of the relevant E^o values, that the dichromate(VI) ion, Cr2O7^2−: • i can be reduced to Cr^3+ and Cr^2+ ions using zinc in acidic conditions • ii can be produced by the oxidation of Cr^3+ ions using hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions (followed by acidification)
statementText.15.23: know that the dichromate(VI) ion, Cr2O7^2−, can be converted into chromate(VI) ions as a result of the equilibrium 2CrO4^2−+ 2H^+ ⇌ Cr2O7^2−+ H2O
statementText.15.24: be able to record observations and write suitable equations for the reactions of Cr^3+(aq), Fe^2+(aq), Fe^3+(aq), Co^2+(aq) and Cu^2+(aq) with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia, including in excess
statementText.15.25: be able to write ionic equations to show the difference between ligand exchange and amphoteric behaviour for the reactions in (24) above
statementText.15.26: understand that ligand exchange, and an accompanying colour change, occurs in the formation of: • i [Cu(ΝΗ3)4(Η2Ο)2]^2+ from [Cu(Η2Ο)6]^2+ via Cu(OH)2(Η2Ο)4 • ii [CuCl4]^2− from [Cu(Η2Ο)6]^2+ • iii [CoCl4]^2− from [Co(Η2Ο)6]^2+
statementText.15.27: understand that the substitution of small, uncharged ligands (such as H2O) by larger, charged ligands (such as Cl^−) can lead to a change in coordination number
statementText.15.28: understand, in terms of the large positive increase in ΔSsystem, that the substitution of a monodentate ligand by a bidentate or multidentate ligand leads to a more stable complex ion
statementText.15.29: know that transition metals and their compounds can act as heterogeneous and homogeneous catalysts
statementText.15.30: know that a heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants and that the reaction occurs at the surface of the catalyst
statementText.15.31: understand, in terms of oxidation number, how V2O5 acts as a catalyst in the contact process
statementText.15.32: understand how a catalytic converter decreases carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide emissions from internal combustion engines by: • i adsorption of CO and NO molecules onto the surface of the catalyst • ii weakening of bonds and chemical reaction • iii desorption of CO2 and N2 product molecules from the surface of the catalyst
statementText.15.33: know that a homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants and appreciate that the catalysed reaction will proceed via an intermediate species
statementText.15.34: understand the role of Fe^2+ ions in catalysing the reaction between I^− and S2O8^2− ions
statementText.15.35: know the role of Mn^2+ ions in autocatalysing the reaction between MnO4^− and C2O4^2− ions

statementText.16.1: understand the terms: • i rate of reaction • ii rate equation • iii order with respect to a substance in a rate equation • iv overall order of reaction • v rate constant • vi half-life • vii rate-determining step • viii activation energy • ix heterogeneous and homogenous catalyst
statementText.16.2: be able to determine and use rate equations of the form: rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where m and n are 0, 1 or 2
statementText.16.3: be able to select and justify a suitable experimental technique to obtain rate data for a given reaction, including: • i titration • ii colorimetry • iii mass change • iv volume of gas evolved • v other suitable technique(s) for a given reaction
statementText.16.4: understand experiments that can be used to investigate reaction rates by: • i an initial-rate method, carrying out separate experiments where different initial concentrations of one reagent are used • ii a continuous monitoring method to generate data to enable concentration- time or volume-time graphs to be plotted [A ‘clock reaction’ is an acceptable approximation of this method]
statementText.16.5: be able to calculate the rate of reaction and the half-life of a first-order reaction using data from a concentration-time or a volume-time graph
statementText.16.6: be able to deduce the order (0, 1 or 2) with respect to a substance in a rate equation using data from: • i a concentration-time graph • ii a rate-concentration graph
statementText.16.7: be able to deduce the order (0, 1 or 2) with respect to a substance in a rate equation using data from an initial-rate method
statementText.16.8: understand how to: • i obtain data to calculate the order with respect to the reactants (and the hydrogen ion) in the acid-catalysed iodination of propanone • ii use these data to make predictions about species involved in the rate-determining step • iii deduce a possible mechanism for the reaction
statementText.16.9: be able to deduce a rate-determining step from a rate equation and vice versa
statementText.16.10: be able to deduce a reaction mechanism, using knowledge from a rate equation and the stoichiometric equation for a reaction
statementText.16.11: understand that knowledge of the rate equations for the hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes can be used to provide evidence for SN1 or SN2 mechanisms for tertiary and primary halogenoalkane hydrolysis
statementText.16.12: be able to use graphical methods to find the activation energy for a reaction from experimental data [The Arrhenius equation will be given if needed.]

statementText.17.1: know that optical isomerism is a result of chirality in molecules with a single chiral centre
statementText.17.2: understand that optical isomerism results from chiral centre(s) in a molecule with asymmetric carbon atom(s) and that optical isomers are object and non- superimposable mirror images
statementText.17.3: know that optical activity is the ability of a single optical isomer to rotate the plane of polarisation of plane-polarised monochromatic light in molecules containing a single chiral centre
statementText.17.4: understand the nature of a racemic mixture
statementText.17.5: be able to use data on optical activity of reactants and products as evidence for SN1 and SN2 mechanisms

statementText.17.6: be able to identify the aldehyde and ketone functional groups
statementText.17.7: understand that aldehydes and ketones: • i do not form intermolecular hydrogen bonds and this affects their physical properties • ii can form hydrogen bonds with water and this affects their solubility
statementText.17.8: understand the reactions of carbonyl compounds with: • i Fehling’s or Benedict’s solution, Tollens’ reagent and acidified dichromate(VI) ions • ii lithium tetrahydridoaluminate (lithium aluminium hydride) in dry ether • iii HCN, in the presence of KCN, as a nucleophilic addition reaction, using curly arrows, relevant lone pairs, dipoles and evidence of optical activity to show the mechanism • iv 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH), as a qualitative test for the presence of a carbonyl group and to identify a carbonyl compound given data for the melting temperatures of derivatives • v iodine in the presence of alkali [In equations, the oxidising agent can be represented as [O] In equations, the reducing agent can be represented as [H] The equation for this reaction is not required]

statementText.17.9: be able to identify the carboxylic acid functional group
statementText.17.10: understand that hydrogen bonding affects the physical properties of carboxylic acids, in relation to their boiling temperatures and solubility
statementText.17.11: understand that carboxylic acids can be prepared by the oxidation of alcohols or aldehydes, and the hydrolysis of nitriles
statementText.17.12: understand the reactions of carboxylic acids with: • i lithium tetrahydridoaluminate (lithium aluminium hydride) in dry ether • ii bases to produce salts • iii phosphorus(V) chloride (phosphorus pentachloride) • iv alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst
statementText.17.13: be able to identify the acyl chloride and ester functional groups
statementText.17.14: understand the reactions of acyl chlorides with: • i water • ii alcohols • iii concentrated ammonia • iv amines
statementText.17.15: understand the hydrolysis reactions of esters, in acidic and alkaline solution
statementText.17.16: understand how polyesters are formed by condensation polymerisation reactions

statementText.18.1: understand that the bonding in benzene has been represented using the Kekulé and the delocalised model, the latter in terms of overlap of p-orbitals to form π-bonds
statementText.18.2: understand that evidence for the delocalised model of the bonding in benzene is provided by data from enthalpy changes of hydrogenation and carbon-carbon bond lengths [Students may represent the structure of benzene as: or as appropriate in equations and mechanisms.]
statementText.18.3: understand why benzene is resistant to bromination, compared with alkenes, in terms of delocalisation of π-bonds in benzene and the localised electron density of the π-bond in alkenes
statementText.18.4: understand the reactions of benzene with: • i oxygen in air (combustion with a smoky flame) • ii bromine, in the presence of a catalyst • iii a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids • iv halogenoalkanes and acyl chlorides with aluminium chloride as catalyst (Friedel-Crafts reaction)
statementText.18.5: understand the mechanism of the electrophilic substitution reactions of benzene (halogenation, nitration and Friedel-Crafts reactions), including the generation of the electrophile
statementText.18.6: understand the reaction of phenol with bromine water
statementText.18.7: understand reasons for the relative ease of bromination of phenol, compared to benzene

name: Amines, amides, amino acids and proteins

statementText.18.8: be able to identify: • i the amine and amide functional groups • ii molecules that are amino acids
statementText.18.9: understand the reactions of primary aliphatic amines, using butylamine as an example, with: • i water to form an alkaline solution • ii acids to form salts • iii ethanoyl chloride • iv halogenoalkanes • v copper(II) ions to form complex ions
statementText.18.10: understand reasons for the difference in basicity of ammonia, primary aliphatic and primary aromatic amines given suitable data
statementText.18.11: understand, in terms of reagents and general reaction conditions, the preparation of primary aliphatic amines: • i from halogenoalkanes • ii by the reduction of nitriles
statementText.18.12: know that aromatic nitro-compounds can be reduced, using tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, to form amines
statementText.18.13: understand that amides can be prepared from acyl chlorides
statementText.18.14: know that the formation of a polyamide is a condensation polymerisation reaction
statementText.18.15: be able to draw the structural formulae of the repeat units of condensation polymers formed by reactions between: • i dicarboxylic acids and diols • ii dicarboxylic acids and diamines • iii amino acids
statementText.18.16: understand the properties of 2-amino acids, including: • i acidity and basicity in solution, as a result of the formation of zwitterions • ii effect of aqueous solutions on plane-polarised monochromatic light
statementText.18.17: understand that the peptide bond in proteins: • i is formed when amino acids combine, by condensation polymerisation • ii can be hydrolysed to form the constituent amino acids, which can be separated by chromatography

statementText.18.18: be able to deduce the empirical formulae, molecular formulae and structural formulae of compounds from data obtained from combustion analysis, elemental percentage composition, characteristic reactions of functional groups, infrared spectra, mass spectra and nuclear magnetic resonance
statementText.18.19: be able to plan reaction schemes, of up to four steps, to form both familiar and unfamiliar compounds
statementText.18.20: understand methods of increasing the length of the carbon chain in a molecule by the use of magnesium to form Grignard reagents and the reactions of the latter with carbon dioxide and with carbonyl compounds in dry ether
statementText.18.21: be able to select and justify suitable practical procedures for carrying out reactions involving compounds with functional groups included in the specification, including identifying appropriate control measures to reduce risk, based on data about hazards
statementText.18.22: understand the following techniques used in the preparation and purification of organic compounds: • i refluxing • ii purification by washing • iii solvent extraction • iv recrystallisation • v drying • vi distillation, including steam distillation • vii melting temperature determination • viii boiling temperature determination

name: Modern analytical techniques II: NMR, mass spectrometry and chromatography

statementText.19.1: be able to use data from mass spectra to: • i suggest possible structures of a simple organic compound given relative molecular masses, accurate to four decimal places • ii calculate the accurate relative molecular mass of a compound, given relative atomic masses to four decimal places, and therefore identify a compound
statementText.19.2: understand that ^13C NMR spectroscopy provides information about the positions of ^13C atoms in a molecule
statementText.19.3: be able to use data from ^13C NMR spectroscopy to: • i predict the different environments for carbon atoms present in a molecule, given values of chemical shift, δ • ii justify the number of peaks present in a ^13C NMR spectrum because of carbon atoms in different environments
statementText.19.4: understand that high resolution proton NMR provides information about the positions of ^1H atoms in a molecule
statementText.19.5: be able to use data from high resolution ^1H NMR spectroscopy to: • i predict the different types of proton present in a molecule, given values of chemical shift, δ • ii relate relative peak areas, or ratio numbers of protons, to the relative numbers of ^1H atoms in different environments • iii deduce the splitting patterns of adjacent, non-equivalent protons using the (n+1) rule and hence suggest the possible structures for a molecule • iv predict the chemical shifts and splitting patterns of the ^1H atoms in a given molecule
statementText.19.6: know that chromatography separates components of a mixture between a mobile phase and a stationary phase
statementText.19.7: be able to calculate Rf values from one-way chromatograms
statementText.19.8: know that high performance liquid chromatography, HPLC, and gas chromatography, GC: • i are types of column chromatography • ii separate substances because of different retention times in the column • iii may be used in conjunction with mass spectrometry, in applications such as forensics or drugs testing in sport
